options: Whether units actually complied with the treatment
The groups to which they were originally randomized, regardless of compliance
Their position relative to the cutoff
questions.explanation: ITT analyzes units by assigned group to preserve the benefits of randomization, giving the policy-relevant effect of offering the program.

questions.q: Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) estimated via IV applies to:
options: 'Compliers' whose treatment status is shifted by the instrument
Only units at the RDD cutoff
questions.explanation: IV recovers the LATE: the effect for compliers who take up treatment because of the instrument, not for always-takers or never-takers.

questions.q: A 'sharp' regression discontinuity design differs from a 'fuzzy' one in that:
options: Sharp RDD has perfect compliance at the cutoff, fuzzy RDD has imperfect compliance
Sharp RDD uses a wider bandwidth
Sharp RDD has no running variable
questions.explanation: In sharp RDD treatment changes deterministically at the cutoff; in fuzzy RDD the probability of treatment jumps but not from 0 to 1, requiring an IV-style adjustment.

questions.q: The main external-validity concern with RDD estimates is that they:
options: Identify a local effect only for units near the cutoff, which may not generalize
questions.explanation: RDD yields a local treatment effect valid at the threshold; the effect may differ for units far from the cutoff, limiting generalization.

questions.q: A staggered rollout of a program across districts over time is often exploited using:
options: Difference-in-differences with variation in treatment timing
questions.explanation: Phased-in program timing provides a natural comparison structure well suited to DiD-style estimation exploiting who is treated when.

questions.q: 'Regression to the mean' can create a false impression of impact when:
options: Units are selected because of extreme baseline values and naturally move toward the average
The comparison group is perfectly matched
questions.explanation: Selecting the worst-performing units at baseline means their later scores tend to improve toward the mean even without any intervention, mimicking an effect.

questions.q: Which is a threat to internal validity rather than external validity?
options: The study population differs from the national population
The intervention was tested only in one season
Findings from an urban pilot may not hold in rural areas
A confounding variable differs between treatment and comparison groups
questions.explanation: Confounding that biases the within-study causal estimate is an internal-validity threat; the others concern generalization.

questions.q: In contribution analysis, 'other influencing factors' should be:
options: Ignored so as to keep the contribution story simple
Explicitly identified and assessed to strengthen or qualify the contribution claim
questions.explanation: Contribution analysis strengthens its causal story precisely by acknowledging and examining alternative explanations and external factors.

questions.q: A 'plausible contribution claim' is one that:
options: Proves the program caused all of the observed change
Is based solely on stakeholder opinion
A reasonable person would accept given the evidence and the ruling out of alternatives
questions.explanation: Contribution analysis aims for claims credible to a reasonable observer, supported by evidence and consideration of rival explanations, not statistical proof of attribution.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the trade-off between internal and external validity?
options: External validity is only relevant for qualitative studies
Tightly controlled studies with high internal validity may be conducted in atypical conditions that limit generalizability
Higher internal validity always guarantees higher external validity
Internal validity concerns sample size, external validity concerns bias
questions.explanation: Efficacy trials under controlled conditions maximize internal validity but their special settings can reduce how well results generalize to real-world contexts.

questions.q: A 'pipeline' comparison group in an evaluation consists of:
options: Future beneficiaries not yet enrolled, used as a comparison for current beneficiaries
Units just below the RDD cutoff
questions.explanation: A pipeline design uses those scheduled to receive the program later as a comparison group, assuming they are similar to current participants.

questions.q: The 'stable unit treatment value assumption' (SUTVA) requires that:
options: One unit's outcome is unaffected by another unit's treatment status, and treatment is well-defined
questions.explanation: SUTVA rules out interference/spillovers between units and requires a single, consistent version of the treatment for valid causal inference.

questions.q: A most-appropriate use of developmental evaluation would be:
options: A routine annual compliance audit of a stable feeding program
A summative impact assessment for a donor's final report
Supporting a social innovation lab piloting new approaches to reduce urban homelessness
Verifying whether output targets were met
questions.explanation: Developmental evaluation fits innovative, adaptive initiatives where goals and strategies are emerging and real-time feedback drives ongoing design.

questions.q: In a DiD study, a placebo (falsification) test often checks whether:
options: There is a 'treatment effect' in a pre-treatment period when there should be none
questions.explanation: Finding a spurious effect before treatment began signals a violation of parallel trends, undermining the DiD design.

questions.q: 'Common support' (overlap) in propensity score matching means:
options: The instrument affects the outcome only through treatment
Both groups experienced the same time trend
There is a region of propensity scores where both treated and untreated units exist
Treatment was randomly assigned within blocks
questions.explanation: Matching requires overlap in propensity scores so that each treated unit has comparable untreated units; observations off common support cannot be matched.

questions.q: Which best describes 'selection on unobservables'?
options: Bias from a poorly worded survey question
Bias from characteristics that determine both participation and outcomes but are not measured
questions.explanation: Selection on unobservables occurs when unmeasured traits (e.g., motivation) drive both program uptake and outcomes, which matching cannot address but randomization can.

questions.q: A key reason RCTs may be considered inappropriate or unethical is:
options: They always cost less than other designs
Withholding a known-beneficial intervention from a control group raises ethical concerns
questions.explanation: When an intervention is already known to help, denying it to a control group can be unethical, so alternative designs may be preferred.

questions.q: The main advantage of a mixed-methods evaluation combining an RCT with qualitative process tracing is that it:
options: Estimates the size of the effect while also explaining the mechanism behind it
Removes the need for a comparison group
questions.explanation: Combining experimental impact estimates with mechanism-focused qualitative work answers both 'did it work' and 'how and why', strengthening causal understanding.

questions.q: When an evaluation asks 'To what extent did our program, alongside other actors, contribute to a policy change?', the most fitting approach is:
questions.explanation: For complex, multi-actor outcomes like policy change where a counterfactual is infeasible, contribution analysis and process tracing assess the program's causal role.

questions.q: A program targets the 20% poorest households using a proxy-means test score; an evaluator finds households bunching just below the eligibility cutoff. This suggests:
options: Manipulation of the running variable, threatening the RDD's validity
The parallel trends assumption is satisfied
questions.explanation: Bunching (a density discontinuity) at the threshold indicates units may be manipulating the score, violating the RDD assumption that assignment is as-good-as-random near the cutoff.

questions.q: In an in-depth interview (IDI), what distinguishes it most clearly from a survey questionnaire?
options: It always involves more than ten respondents at once
It uses open-ended questions and follow-up probes to explore meaning in depth
It produces numerical scores for statistical analysis
It must be conducted only by the principal investigator
questions.explanation: IDIs rely on open-ended questions and probes to explore a single respondent's perspectives and experiences in depth rather than generating quantifiable scores.

questions.q: A 'key informant' in a key informant interview (KII) is best defined as someone who:
options: Represents a random cross-section of the target population
Is selected because they are easiest to reach
Has specialised knowledge or a strategic vantage point on the topic
questions.explanation: Key informants are chosen for their specialised knowledge or strategic position, not for statistical representativeness.

questions.q: The ideal size for most focus group discussions (FGDs) is generally considered to be:
questions.explanation: Most FGD guidance recommends 6 to 10 participants so that everyone can contribute while still allowing group interaction.

questions.q: A distinctive analytical value of the FGD over individual interviews is that it:
options: Eliminates the need for a moderator
Generates data from participant interaction and the negotiation of shared meanings
questions.explanation: The FGD's unique strength is the group interaction, where participants build on, challenge, and negotiate meanings with each other.

questions.q: In participant observation, 'going native' refers to the risk that the researcher:
options: Loses analytical distance by over-identifying with the group studied
questions.explanation: 'Going native' is the loss of critical, analytic distance when a researcher over-identifies with the community being observed.

questions.q: The Most Significant Change (MSC) technique is best described as:
options: A statistical regression of programme outcomes
A participatory, story-based monitoring approach that collects and selects significant-change stories
A structured survey administered at baseline and endline
questions.explanation: MSC is a participatory technique that gathers stories of significant change and uses systematic selection to surface what stakeholders value most.

questions.q: Outcome Harvesting is particularly suited to situations where:
options: Change is complex and outcomes cannot be fully predicted in advance
Outcomes are pre-defined and easily counted at baseline
Random assignment to treatment is possible
questions.explanation: Outcome Harvesting works backwards from observed changes, making it ideal for complex settings where outcomes are emergent and not predictable.

questions.q: In Outcome Harvesting, a well-formulated outcome description must include:
options: A description of who changed, what changed, and the contribution of the intervention
questions.explanation: An Outcome Harvesting outcome statement specifies the social actor, the observable change in behaviour/relationships/actions, and how the intervention contributed.

questions.q: Purposive sampling in qualitative research means selecting participants because they:
options: Are chosen by a random-number generator
Volunteer through a public advertisement only
Meet specific criteria relevant to the research question
questions.explanation: Purposive (purposeful) sampling deliberately selects information-rich cases that meet criteria relevant to the study's questions.

questions.q: Theoretical sampling, as used in grounded theory, is driven by:
options: A fixed sample size set before data collection begins
The emerging theory, where subsequent cases are chosen to develop and test concepts
questions.explanation: In theoretical sampling, ongoing analysis directs the researcher to the next cases needed to elaborate and refine the developing theory.

questions.q: Data saturation in qualitative research is reached when:
options: A predetermined number of interviews has been completed
The budget for fieldwork is exhausted
No substantially new codes, themes, or insights emerge from additional data
All participants give the same demographic details
questions.explanation: Saturation is the point at which additional data collection yields no new themes or insights, indicating analytical completeness.

questions.q: Which sampling approach selects 'extreme or deviant cases' to learn from unusual manifestations of a phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Extreme or deviant case sampling deliberately targets outliers to illuminate what makes a phenomenon distinctive.

questions.q: Maximum variation sampling is used primarily to:
options: Minimise the range of perspectives collected
Capture and describe central themes that cut across a wide range of diverse cases
Reduce the number of interviews needed to two
questions.explanation: Maximum variation sampling intentionally includes diverse cases so that common patterns emerging across them carry particular significance.

questions.q: In coding, an INDUCTIVE (data-driven) approach means that:
options: Codes are fixed before reading any transcripts
Codes are derived from the data itself rather than a pre-existing framework
questions.explanation: Inductive coding builds codes bottom-up from the data, letting categories emerge rather than imposing a prior framework.

questions.q: A DEDUCTIVE (concept-driven) coding approach begins with:
options: A statistical model of the outcomes
A predefined codebook or theoretical framework applied to the data
questions.explanation: Deductive coding starts from an existing theory or codebook and applies those a priori codes to the data.

questions.q: In grounded theory, 'open coding' refers to:
options: Linking categories to subcategories around a core phenomenon
Deleting all codes that appear only once
Breaking data into discrete parts and labelling them with initial conceptual codes
questions.explanation: Open coding is the first analytic step of fragmenting data and assigning initial conceptual labels.

questions.q: 'Axial coding' in grounded theory involves:
options: Relating categories to their subcategories to identify connections and conditions
questions.explanation: Axial coding reassembles data by linking categories and subcategories, examining conditions, contexts, and consequences.

questions.q: Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis defines a 'theme' as something that:
options: Captures something important about the data in relation to the research question and represents a patterned response
Is any single word repeated three times
Must be quantified as a percentage
questions.explanation: For Braun and Clarke, a theme captures a patterned meaning that is important relative to the research question, not merely something frequent.

questions.q: The correct order of the first three phases in Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis is:
options: Writing up, reviewing themes, defining themes
Familiarisation, generating initial codes, searching for themes
questions.explanation: The six phases begin with familiarising yourself with the data, generating initial codes, then searching for themes.

questions.q: Triangulation in qualitative research primarily serves to:
options: Replace the need for informed consent
Enhance credibility by examining a phenomenon from multiple sources, methods, or perspectives
questions.explanation: Triangulation uses multiple data sources, methods, investigators, or theories to strengthen the credibility of findings.

questions.q: Using both FGDs and household interviews to study the same question is an example of:
questions.explanation: Methodological triangulation combines different data-collection methods to study the same phenomenon.

questions.q: When two or more researchers independently analyse the same data and compare interpretations, this is:
questions.explanation: Investigator triangulation involves multiple analysts to reduce individual bias and check interpretations.

questions.q: In Lincoln and Guba's framework, 'credibility' is the qualitative analogue of which conventional criterion?
questions.explanation: Credibility parallels internal validity, addressing whether findings accurately represent participants' realities.

questions.q: 'Transferability' in Lincoln and Guba's trustworthiness framework corresponds to:
questions.explanation: Transferability parallels external validity, concerning the extent findings may apply to other contexts, supported by thick description.

questions.q: 'Dependability' in the trustworthiness framework is the analogue of:
questions.explanation: Dependability parallels reliability, focusing on the consistency and traceability of the research process over time.

questions.q: 'Confirmability' addresses the concern that findings are:
options: Shaped by respondents and the inquiry rather than the researcher's bias or motivation
questions.explanation: Confirmability, the analogue of objectivity, ensures findings are grounded in the data rather than the investigator's predispositions.

questions.q: 'Member checking' is a technique to strengthen credibility by:
options: Adding more interviewers to the team
Returning findings or interpretations to participants for verification
questions.explanation: Member checking asks participants to review data, interpretations, or conclusions to confirm they resonate with their experience.

questions.q: 'Thick description', a term associated with Geertz and used by Lincoln and Guba, mainly supports:
questions.explanation: Rich, contextualised (thick) description lets readers judge whether findings might transfer to their own settings.

questions.q: An 'audit trail' in qualitative research primarily supports which trustworthiness criteria?
questions.explanation: A documented audit trail of decisions and raw materials lets an external reviewer confirm dependability and confirmability.

questions.q: Reflexivity in qualitative research refers to:
options: Critical self-examination of how the researcher's positionality and assumptions shape the inquiry
The speed at which a researcher records notes
The automatic coding done by software
questions.explanation: Reflexivity is the researcher's ongoing critical reflection on how their identity, values, and role influence data and interpretation.

questions.q: A 'reflexive journal' is most directly used to:
options: Record the researcher's evolving thoughts, decisions, and potential biases during fieldwork
questions.explanation: A reflexive journal documents the researcher's reflections and methodological decisions, aiding both reflexivity and the audit trail.

questions.q: A MEL officer wants to understand WHY beneficiaries in a livelihoods programme dropped out. The most appropriate first method is:
options: In-depth interviews with a purposive sample of dropouts
A large-scale structured survey with closed questions
questions.explanation: IDIs with purposively selected dropouts are best suited to explore the 'why' and lived reasons behind attrition.

questions.q: During an FGD on sensitive gender norms, the moderator notices two dominant participants silencing others. The best immediate response is to:
options: Ignore it and rely on the dominant voices
Convert the FGD into a survey on the spot
Actively redirect and invite quieter participants to share, managing group dynamics
questions.explanation: Skilled moderation manages group dynamics by drawing out quieter members so the data reflects the range of views, not just dominant ones.

questions.q: A team finds that after 18 interviews no new themes are appearing, but the plan specified 30. The methodologically sound decision is to:
options: Consider that saturation may be reached and justify stopping, documenting the rationale
Stop only when exactly 30 are done regardless of saturation
questions.explanation: Saturation, not a fixed target, governs sample adequacy in qualitative inquiry; stopping should be justified and documented.

questions.q: An evaluator wants to select villages for case studies that differ widely in remoteness, caste composition, and market access to see if common patterns hold. This is:
questions.explanation: Deliberately choosing diverse cases to find patterns that cut across them is maximum variation sampling.

questions.q: A researcher studying an underground sex-worker collective recruits new participants through referrals from existing ones. This is:
questions.explanation: Snowball sampling uses referrals from existing participants to reach hidden or hard-to-access populations.

questions.q: When coding transcripts, a MEL analyst applies a pre-agreed codebook from the theory of change but also adds new codes for unexpected content. This hybrid approach is best called:
questions.explanation: Combining an a priori codebook with emergent codes from the data is a hybrid deductive-inductive strategy.

questions.q: 'In vivo' coding assigns codes that:
options: Are drawn from the exact words or phrases used by participants
Are generated automatically by frequency counts
questions.explanation: In vivo codes use participants' own language, preserving their voice and meaning.

questions.q: To improve dependability, a two-person coding team calculates the proportion of segments they coded identically. This measure is:
questions.explanation: Inter-coder reliability quantifies agreement between coders, supporting the consistency (dependability) of coding.

questions.q: A donor asks whether IDI findings from three districts apply to a fourth. The evaluator's most defensible response is to:
options: Claim automatic generalisability to all districts
Refuse to comment on transferability at all
Provide thick description of the studied contexts so the donor can judge transferability
questions.explanation: Qualitative transferability is judged by the reader using thick contextual description, not asserted as statistical generalisation.

questions.q: In an MSC process, the SELECTION of significant-change stories at each level is typically done by:
options: Stakeholder panels who discuss and choose stories according to agreed domains and criteria
questions.explanation: In MSC, panels of stakeholders deliberate and select the most significant stories, making values and criteria explicit.

questions.q: A key strength of Outcome Harvesting's 'substantiation' step is that it:
options: Removes the need for any evidence
Uses independent sources to verify the accuracy of harvested outcomes
questions.explanation: Substantiation asks independent, knowledgeable third parties to verify harvested outcomes, strengthening credibility.

questions.q: Outcome Harvesting typically speaks of the intervention's 'contribution' rather than 'attribution' because:
options: In complex settings multiple factors drive change and sole causal claims are rarely defensible
questions.explanation: In complex environments many actors and factors interact, so plausible contribution is more defensible than sole attribution.

questions.q: A participant-observer records factual field notes separately from personal reflections and analytic hunches. Keeping these separate mainly improves:
options: Confirmability, by distinguishing observed data from interpretation
questions.explanation: Separating descriptive notes from interpretive memos keeps interpretation traceable to data, supporting confirmability.

questions.q: 'Prolonged engagement' in the field primarily contributes to credibility by:
options: Building trust and understanding context well enough to distinguish salient from distorting information
Reducing the number of participants required
questions.explanation: Prolonged engagement builds rapport and contextual understanding, helping the researcher recognise and rule out distortions.

questions.q: 'Negative case analysis' strengthens qualitative rigour by:
options: Deleting data that disagrees with the emerging theory
Actively seeking and accounting for cases that contradict the developing interpretation
questions.explanation: Negative case analysis deliberately examines disconfirming evidence and refines interpretations to fit all data.

questions.q: A study reports its coding scheme, decision log, raw transcripts, and memos so an external reviewer could follow the analytic path. This documentation is the:
questions.explanation: An audit trail is the systematic record of data, decisions, and processes enabling external verification.

questions.q: When a KII respondent gives information that contradicts programme monitoring data, the best analytic step is to:
options: Automatically trust the monitoring data and discard the KII
Treat the discrepancy as a lead to investigate through further triangulation
Report only the KII because it is qualitative
questions.explanation: Discrepancies between sources are analytic opportunities; triangulation is used to explore and explain them rather than discard data.

questions.q: An evaluator wants participants themselves to interpret change stories in their own words for a learning workshop. Which method best fits?
options: Most Significant Change, using participant-selected stories
questions.explanation: MSC centres participant-generated and participant-selected change stories, making it ideal for participatory learning.

questions.q: A common threat to FGD data quality is 'social desirability bias', which means participants:
options: Answer in ways they think are socially acceptable rather than their true views
Speak in a language the moderator cannot understand
questions.explanation: Social desirability bias leads participants to give answers they believe are approved of, especially on sensitive topics in a group.

questions.q: A survey records respondents' districts (e.g., Dhaka, Colombo, Kathmandu). What level of measurement is this variable?
questions.explanation: District names are categories with no inherent order, which is the defining feature of a nominal variable.

questions.q: A beneficiary satisfaction scale runs from 'Very dissatisfied' to 'Very satisfied'. What is its level of measurement?
questions.explanation: Ordered categories with unequal or unknown spacing between them constitute an ordinal variable.

questions.q: Which variable is measured at the ratio level?
questions.explanation: Income has a true zero and equal intervals, making it a ratio variable where ratios (twice as much) are meaningful.

questions.q: Temperature measured in degrees Celsius is an example of which level of measurement?
questions.explanation: Celsius has equal intervals but an arbitrary zero point, so it is interval, not ratio.

questions.q: For a strongly right-skewed income distribution, which measure of central tendency best represents the 'typical' value?
questions.explanation: The median resists the pull of extreme high values, making it more representative than the mean for skewed income data.

questions.q: Which statistic is defined as the most frequently occurring value in a dataset?
questions.explanation: The mode is the value that appears most often and is the only central-tendency measure usable for nominal data.

questions.q: The standard deviation is best described as:
options: The average distance of values from the mean
The middle value of the dataset
The difference between the largest and smallest values
questions.explanation: Standard deviation summarizes typical spread as the square root of the average squared deviation from the mean.

questions.q: If every value in a dataset is multiplied by 10, what happens to the standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation scales linearly, so multiplying all values by a constant multiplies the SD by the same constant.

questions.q: The interquartile range (IQR) is calculated as:
options: The square of the standard deviation
questions.explanation: The IQR is the spread of the middle 50% of data, found by subtracting the first quartile from the third.

questions.q: Variance is related to standard deviation in that:
options: Variance is the square root of the standard deviation
Variance is the standard deviation squared
Variance is the standard deviation divided by n
questions.explanation: Variance equals the standard deviation squared, expressed in squared units of the original measure.

questions.q: A distribution where the mean is substantially greater than the median is most likely:
questions.explanation: In a right-skewed distribution, a long upper tail pulls the mean above the median.

questions.q: In a perfectly symmetric, unimodal distribution, the mean, median, and mode are:
options: In the order mean < median < mode
questions.explanation: Symmetry and a single peak cause the three measures of central tendency to coincide.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean in a normal distribution?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule states roughly 68% of a normal distribution lies within one SD of the mean.

questions.q: A cross-tabulation (contingency table) is primarily used to:
options: Examine the relationship between two categorical variables
Calculate a confidence interval for a proportion
questions.explanation: Cross-tabs display joint frequencies of two categorical variables to reveal association patterns.

questions.q: In a 2x2 cross-tabulation of program participation and employment status, which statistical test is most appropriate to assess association?
questions.explanation: The chi-square test of independence assesses whether two categorical variables are associated.

questions.q: The statement 'correlation does not imply causation' warns that:
options: Correlated variables can never be causally related
An observed association may be due to confounding or coincidence rather than a causal link
Causation can only be shown with large samples
questions.explanation: Two variables can move together because of a lurking confounder, reverse causation, or chance, not necessarily a direct causal effect.

questions.q: A Pearson correlation coefficient of -0.85 indicates:
questions.explanation: Values near -1 indicate a strong inverse linear association between the two variables.

questions.q: Which correlation coefficient represents the weakest linear relationship?
questions.explanation: The strength of a linear relationship depends on the absolute value, so 0.05 is closest to zero and weakest.

questions.q: A confounding variable in an evaluation is one that:
options: Is related to both the intervention and the outcome, distorting their apparent relationship
Has no effect on the outcome
questions.explanation: A confounder is associated with both exposure and outcome, biasing the estimated effect if not controlled.

questions.q: In hypothesis testing, the null hypothesis typically states that:
options: There is a significant effect or difference
There is no effect or no difference
questions.explanation: The null hypothesis is the default of no effect or no difference that the test seeks to reject.

questions.q: A p-value of 0.03 in a two-sided test at the 0.05 significance level means you should:
options: Fail to reject the null hypothesis
Accept the null hypothesis as proven
Increase the sample size before deciding
questions.explanation: Because 0.03 is below the 0.05 threshold, the result is statistically significant and the null is rejected.

questions.q: A p-value is best interpreted as:
options: The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability of observing data as extreme as the sample, assuming the null hypothesis is true
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true
The size of the treatment effect
questions.explanation: The p-value is the probability, under the null, of results at least as extreme as those observed.

questions.q: A Type I error occurs when a researcher:
options: Fails to reject a false null hypothesis
questions.explanation: A Type I error is a false positive: concluding an effect exists when it does not.

questions.q: A Type II error occurs when a researcher:
options: Fails to reject a false null hypothesis
Sets the significance level too low
questions.explanation: A Type II error is a false negative: missing a real effect by failing to reject a false null.

questions.q: The significance level (alpha) of a test represents:
options: The probability of a Type II error
The probability of a Type I error the researcher is willing to accept
questions.explanation: Alpha is the pre-set maximum probability of wrongly rejecting a true null hypothesis.

questions.q: Statistical power is defined as the probability of:
options: Correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis
questions.explanation: Power equals 1 minus the Type II error rate: the chance of detecting a true effect.

questions.q: Which factor generally increases the statistical power of a test?
questions.explanation: Larger samples reduce sampling variability, increasing the ability to detect true effects.

questions.q: An independent-samples t-test is used to compare:
options: Two proportions from a single group
The means of two independent groups
More than three group means simultaneously
A relationship between two continuous variables
questions.explanation: The independent-samples t-test evaluates whether two separate groups differ in their means.

questions.q: A paired-samples (dependent) t-test is most appropriate when:
options: Comparing means of two unrelated groups
Comparing the same subjects' scores before and after an intervention
Testing association between two categorical variables
Comparing four or more group means
questions.explanation: The paired t-test handles two related measurements, such as pre- and post-test scores on the same people.

questions.q: A one-way ANOVA is used to test:
options: Whether two categorical variables are associated
Whether the means of three or more groups differ
questions.explanation: ANOVA compares means across three or more groups to detect any overall difference.

questions.q: A significant one-way ANOVA result tells you that:
options: All group means differ from each other
At least one group mean differs from the others
The largest group has the highest mean
questions.explanation: A significant F-test indicates at least one mean differs, but post-hoc tests are needed to locate which.

questions.q: The chi-square test of independence assumes that:
options: Data are continuous and normally distributed
Expected cell counts are sufficiently large (commonly at least 5)
questions.explanation: The chi-square approximation requires adequately large expected frequencies, often a minimum of 5 per cell.

questions.q: In simple linear regression, the slope coefficient represents:
options: The predicted value of Y when X is zero
The change in Y for a one-unit change in X
The correlation between X and Y
questions.explanation: The slope quantifies how much the outcome is expected to change per one-unit increase in the predictor.

questions.q: In a regression model, R-squared indicates:
options: The slope of the regression line
The proportion of variance in the outcome explained by the predictors
questions.explanation: R-squared is the share of outcome variance accounted for by the model's predictors.

questions.q: The intercept in a simple linear regression is:
options: The predicted value of Y when all predictors equal zero
The average change in Y per unit X
Always equal to the mean of Y
questions.explanation: The intercept is the model's predicted outcome when the predictor(s) take the value zero.

questions.q: Multiple regression differs from simple regression in that it:
options: Includes two or more predictor variables
questions.explanation: Multiple regression models an outcome using several predictors simultaneously, allowing statistical control.

questions.q: A 95% confidence interval for a mean is best interpreted as:
options: 95% of the data fall within this interval
A range that, over repeated sampling, would contain the true mean 95% of the time
There is a 95% chance the sample mean is correct
The interval contains 95% of possible sample means
questions.explanation: The 95% refers to the long-run capture rate of the true parameter across repeated samples.

questions.q: All else equal, increasing the sample size will make a confidence interval:
questions.explanation: Larger samples reduce the standard error, producing a narrower, more precise interval.

questions.q: A 99% confidence interval, compared with a 95% interval from the same data, will be:
questions.explanation: Higher confidence requires capturing more of the sampling distribution, widening the interval.

questions.q: If a 95% confidence interval for a difference in means is (-0.5 to 3.2), you should conclude that:
options: The difference is statistically significant at the 0.05 level
The difference is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level
The sample size was too large
questions.explanation: Because the interval includes zero, the difference is not significant at the corresponding 0.05 level.

questions.q: Cohen's d is a measure of:
options: Standardized effect size for the difference between two means
questions.explanation: Cohen's d expresses the difference between two means in standard-deviation units, a common effect-size metric.

questions.q: By common convention, a Cohen's d of 0.8 is interpreted as a:
questions.explanation: Cohen's benchmarks label d values around 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, and 0.8 large.

questions.q: Why is effect size important to report alongside a p-value?
options: It replaces the need for a confidence interval
It conveys the practical magnitude of a finding, which significance alone does not
It guarantees the result is causal
questions.explanation: A p-value shows whether an effect is detectable, while effect size shows how large and practically meaningful it is.

questions.q: With a very large sample, a trivially small difference can become statistically significant. This illustrates that:
options: Statistical significance does not guarantee practical importance
questions.explanation: Large samples can detect tiny effects, so significance must be interpreted alongside effect size and context.

questions.q: 'P-hacking' refers to the pitfall of:
options: Reporting confidence intervals instead of p-values
Running many analyses and selectively reporting those that reach significance
questions.explanation: P-hacking inflates false positives by testing many hypotheses and reporting only the significant ones.

questions.q: The ecological fallacy is the error of:
options: Inferring individual-level relationships from group-level (aggregate) data
questions.explanation: The ecological fallacy wrongly assumes aggregate-level associations hold at the individual level.

questions.q: Survivorship bias in M&E data analysis occurs when:
options: Only participants who remained in the program are analyzed, ignoring dropouts
The mean is used instead of the median
questions.explanation: Analyzing only 'survivors' who stayed in a program can badly overstate outcomes by excluding dropouts.

questions.q: An outlier in a dataset is a value that:
options: Lies far from the bulk of the other observations
questions.explanation: An outlier is an unusually extreme value relative to the rest of the data, which may or may not be an error.

questions.q: Which measure of central tendency is most affected by extreme outliers?
questions.explanation: The mean incorporates every value, so extreme observations pull it strongly, unlike the resistant median.

questions.q: Regression to the mean can mislead evaluators when:
options: Participants selected for extreme baseline scores show movement toward average on retest regardless of the intervention
The regression slope is exactly zero
questions.explanation: Groups chosen for extreme initial values tend to move toward the average on remeasurement, which can be mistaken for a program effect.

questions.q: In data quality, 'validity' refers to which characteristic of data?
options: Whether the data measure what they are intended to measure
Whether data are collected on schedule
Whether the same result is obtained on repeated measurement
questions.explanation: Validity is the extent to which data clearly and adequately represent the intended result or indicator being measured.

questions.q: The data quality dimension 'reliability' is best described as:
options: The data reflect the most current situation
The data are collected only once
The data are generated by a consistent, stable process that produces the same result repeatedly
The data have no missing values
questions.explanation: Reliability means the data collection process is consistent and stable, so repeated measurement under the same conditions yields the same results.

questions.q: 'Precision' as a data quality dimension means that data:
options: Have a sufficient level of detail to support management decisions
questions.explanation: Precision (sometimes called granularity) refers to data having enough detail to present an accurate picture and support decision-making.

questions.q: Which data quality dimension is directly compromised when a monitoring officer alters figures in a report to please a donor?
questions.explanation: Integrity concerns whether data are protected from deliberate manipulation or unintentional error for political or personal reasons.

questions.q: 'Timeliness' of data means that data are:
options: Up to date and available when needed for decisions
questions.explanation: Timeliness means data are sufficiently current and available frequently enough to inform management and decision-making.

questions.q: A Data Quality Assessment (DQA) is primarily conducted to:
options: Increase the number of indicators in a results framework
Verify and assess the quality of reported data and the systems that produce them
Replace the need for a baseline survey
questions.explanation: A DQA systematically reviews reported data and the data management systems to assess strengths and weaknesses against quality standards.

questions.q: The five data quality standards most commonly assessed in a USAID-style DQA are validity, integrity, precision, reliability, and:
questions.explanation: The five standard data quality dimensions are validity, integrity, precision, reliability, and timeliness.

questions.q: During a routine data quality audit, an evaluator recounts source documents and compares them to the figure reported to the donor. This step is best described as:
questions.explanation: Trace-and-verify checks re-aggregate source records and compare them against reported values to confirm accuracy.

questions.q: An 'audit trail' in a data management system refers to:
options: A record showing who entered or changed data, when, and what was changed
The route field staff take to reach a village
A list of survey respondents' names
questions.explanation: An audit trail is a chronological record of data entries and modifications, enabling changes to be traced back to their source and author.

questions.q: If a program consistently over-reports beneficiaries because the counting method double-counts people served in two activities, the main data quality problem is with:
options: Validity (the count does not accurately measure unique beneficiaries)
questions.explanation: Double-counting means the reported figure does not validly represent the intended concept of unique individuals reached.

questions.q: Which of the following most improves the reliability of data collected across multiple field sites?
options: Using a different questionnaire at each site
Allowing each enumerator to interpret questions freely
Collecting data only once a year
Standardised data collection tools and enumerator training with clear definitions
questions.explanation: Standardised instruments, definitions, and enumerator training ensure a consistent process that produces comparable, reliable data.

questions.q: A key threat to data integrity in performance monitoring is:
options: Incentives that reward reporting high numbers, creating pressure to inflate results
questions.explanation: Performance pressures and result-linked incentives can motivate manipulation of figures, undermining integrity.

questions.q: The principle of 'informed consent' in research requires that participants:
options: Sign a form regardless of understanding
Understand the purpose, risks, and benefits and agree voluntarily to participate
questions.explanation: Informed consent means participants comprehend what participation involves, including risks and benefits, and agree freely without coercion.

questions.q: 'Voluntary participation' as an ethical principle means that respondents:
options: Must complete the survey once started
May decline to participate or withdraw at any time without penalty
Are required to answer every question
questions.explanation: Voluntary participation ensures individuals can choose not to take part, or to stop, at any point without negative consequences.

questions.q: The ethical principle of 'do no harm' in MEL data collection primarily requires practitioners to:
options: Avoid exposing participants to physical, psychological, social, or economic risk through the research
Complete data collection as quickly as possible
questions.explanation: Do-no-harm requires anticipating and minimising any harm that participation or data use could cause to individuals or communities.

questions.q: What is the key distinction between confidentiality and anonymity?
options: Anonymity means identity is never known to anyone; confidentiality means identity is known but protected from disclosure
Anonymity means the data are deleted immediately
questions.explanation: With anonymity no one can link responses to an individual; with confidentiality the researcher knows the identity but commits to protecting it.

questions.q: A survey where the enumerator records the respondent's name and phone number but promises not to share them is offering:
questions.explanation: Because identity is known to the researcher but protected from others, this is confidentiality, not anonymity.

questions.q: An Institutional Review Board (IRB) or ethics review committee primarily exists to:
options: Review research protocols to protect the rights and welfare of human participants
questions.explanation: An IRB/ethics committee independently reviews research to ensure participant rights, safety, and welfare are protected.

questions.q: Which research would most clearly require prior ethics review before data collection?
options: Analysis of already-published national census tables
Counting the number of trees in a public park
A study collecting sensitive personal accounts of gender-based violence from survivors
Reviewing a project's own budget spreadsheet
questions.explanation: Research involving vulnerable people and sensitive personal data carries higher risk and requires ethics review to safeguard participants.

questions.q: In safeguarding terms, a 'safeguarding concern' involving research participants would include:
options: A respondent giving a short answer
Disclosure of abuse, exploitation, or a risk of harm to a participant during data collection
questions.explanation: Safeguarding concerns arise when data collection surfaces evidence of harm, abuse, or exploitation requiring a protective response.

questions.q: 'Responsible data' practice in the development sector emphasises:
options: Collecting as much personal data as possible for future use
Handling data in ways that respect the rights, dignity, and safety of the people the data are about
Sharing all datasets publicly by default
questions.explanation: Responsible data is about prioritising the rights and wellbeing of data subjects throughout the data lifecycle.

questions.q: India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act was enacted in which year?
questions.explanation: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act was passed in India in 2023.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, the entity that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data is called the:
questions.explanation: The DPDP Act terms the entity deciding the purpose and means of processing a 'Data Fiduciary'.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, the individual to whom the personal data relates is called the:
questions.explanation: The Act refers to the individual whose personal data is processed as the 'Data Principal'.

questions.q: The data protection principle of 'data minimisation' means:
options: Reducing the sample size of surveys
Collecting only the personal data necessary for the specified purpose
Minimising the file size of datasets
Collecting data from the fewest possible districts
questions.explanation: Data minimisation limits collection to what is strictly necessary to achieve the stated purpose.

questions.q: 'Purpose limitation' as a data protection principle requires that personal data:
options: Be used only for the specific purposes for which they were collected and consented to
Be collected in bulk for unspecified future uses
questions.explanation: Purpose limitation restricts use of data to the defined, consented purposes and prohibits incompatible secondary uses.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, processing the personal data of a child generally requires:
options: Verifiable consent of a parent or lawful guardian
Approval of the school principal only
questions.explanation: The DPDP Act requires verifiable parental or guardian consent before processing a child's personal data.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, a 'child' is defined as an individual below the age of:
questions.explanation: The DPDP Act defines a child as any individual who has not completed eighteen years of age.

questions.q: When seeking consent from a vulnerable group with low literacy, best practice is to:
options: Require them to read and sign a lengthy English form
Provide information verbally in the local language and obtain oral or witnessed consent as appropriate
Skip consent because they cannot read
Have a supervisor consent on their behalf
questions.explanation: For low-literacy participants, consent should be explained clearly in the local language, using oral or witnessed procedures to ensure genuine understanding.

questions.q: Obtaining assent from a child in research (in addition to parental consent) means:
options: The child's fingerprint on a legal contract
The child's own age-appropriate agreement to participate
questions.explanation: Assent is the child's affirmative, age-appropriate agreement to take part, sought alongside a guardian's consent.

questions.q: A power imbalance that can undermine truly voluntary consent occurs when:
options: The interviewer is the same age as the respondent
Participants believe that refusing will cost them access to program benefits
The interview is conducted in the local language
questions.explanation: If people fear losing services by declining, their consent is coerced by dependency and not genuinely voluntary.

questions.q: Which practice best protects confidentiality when storing survey data with identifiers?
options: Emailing the full dataset to all partners
Separating direct identifiers from response data and restricting access with encryption/passwords
Printing copies for every staff member
Posting the dataset on a public website
questions.explanation: Separating identifiers, encrypting files, and limiting access reduce the risk of unauthorised disclosure of confidential data.

questions.q: 'De-identification' (anonymisation) of a dataset involves:
options: Removing or masking direct and indirect identifiers so individuals cannot be re-identified
questions.explanation: De-identification strips identifying details so that the data cannot reasonably be linked back to specific individuals.

questions.q: A completeness check on a dataset would flag:
options: Values that are out of the plausible range
Data entered by the wrong enumerator
questions.explanation: Completeness checks identify missing values in required fields, one aspect of overall data quality.

questions.q: A consistency (logic) check in data cleaning would catch which of the following?
options: A respondent recorded as a 5-year-old who is also reported as married with children
An enumerator taking a lunch break
questions.explanation: Consistency checks flag logically incompatible values across fields, such as an age inconsistent with reported life events.

questions.q: The main data quality risk of collecting data long after the reporting period is that it undermines:
questions.explanation: Late data may no longer reflect the current situation or arrive too late for decisions, undermining timeliness.

questions.q: An organisation that keeps personal data 'only as long as necessary' and then securely deletes it is applying the principle of:
questions.explanation: Storage limitation requires retaining personal data only as long as needed for the stated purpose, then deleting it.

questions.q: Which is the strongest example of a data breach requiring response under a responsible-data protocol?
options: A typo in an indicator name
An unencrypted laptop containing beneficiaries' names and health status is stolen
A duplicate row in a spreadsheet
questions.explanation: Loss of a device holding sensitive personal data is a breach that can harm individuals and requires notification and mitigation.

questions.q: In a DQA, weak links between the source records and the reported number most directly threaten:
options: Validity and integrity of reported data
questions.explanation: If reported figures cannot be traced to verifiable source records, both the validity and integrity of the data are in question.

questions.q: A monitoring team finds that two data sources give very different values for the same indicator. The best first step is to:
options: Report the higher figure to look successful
Average the two numbers without checking
Investigate the definitions, methods, and sources to reconcile the discrepancy
questions.explanation: Reconciling discrepancies requires examining definitions and methods to determine the accurate value, protecting validity and integrity.

questions.q: 'Purpose limitation' would be violated if an NGO:
options: Uses attendance data to report training numbers as promised
Deletes data after the retention period
Sells beneficiaries' contact details to a marketing company
questions.explanation: Repurposing personal data for marketing without consent breaches purpose limitation, using data beyond the agreed purpose.

questions.q: When interviewing survivors of trauma, an ethical MEL practitioner should ensure:
options: Referral pathways to support services are available and offered
The interview is recorded on social media
As many probing questions as possible
Names are read aloud in a group setting
questions.explanation: Do-no-harm requires having referral and support mechanisms ready in case participation causes or reveals distress.

questions.q: Which statement about consent forms is correct?
options: A signature always guarantees genuine informed consent
Consent is a process of understanding and agreement, of which the form is only a record
Consent forms are only for donors
Consent must be in English to be valid
questions.explanation: Informed consent is an ongoing process of comprehension and voluntary agreement; the signed form merely documents it.

questions.q: A data 'validity' problem, rather than a reliability problem, is best illustrated by:
options: Two enumerators recording the same weight differently
Using number of trainings held as a proxy for improved knowledge, which it does not truly measure
A scale that gives different readings each time
questions.explanation: Using an indicator that does not actually capture the intended concept is a validity problem, distinct from inconsistent measurement (reliability).

questions.q: Under a responsible-data approach, deciding whether to collect a sensitive variable (e.g., HIV status) should include:
options: Collecting it because it might be useful someday
Assessing whether it is necessary for the purpose and weighing the risk to participants
Collecting it only if storage is cheap
questions.explanation: Sensitive data should be collected only when necessary and justified against the risk of harm to participants (data minimisation and do-no-harm).

questions.q: The DPDP Act 2023 grants Data Principals the right to:
options: Access, correction, and erasure of their personal data
A share of the organisation's profits
questions.explanation: The Act provides individuals rights including access to, correction of, and erasure of their personal data.

questions.q: A 'Significant Data Fiduciary' under the DPDP Act 2023 is subject to additional obligations such as:
options: Appointing a Data Protection Officer and conducting Data Protection Impact Assessments
questions.explanation: Significant Data Fiduciaries face enhanced duties including appointing a DPO and conducting Data Protection Impact Assessments and audits.

questions.q: The safest way to share disaggregated data about a small, identifiable minority group is to:
options: Publish exact counts even if cells contain only one or two people
Suppress or aggregate small cells to prevent re-identification of individuals
questions.explanation: Small-cell suppression or aggregation prevents individuals in tiny subgroups from being re-identified, protecting confidentiality.

questions.q: An audit trail and version control in a data system most directly support which data quality dimension?
questions.explanation: Tracking who changed what and when deters and detects manipulation, protecting the integrity of the data.

questions.q: The best overall summary of ethical MEL data practice is to:
options: Maximise data collection and minimise consent to save time
Prioritise donor reporting over participant welfare
Balance the value of the information with respect for participants' rights, safety, dignity, and privacy throughout the data lifecycle
Avoid documenting consent to reduce paperwork
questions.explanation: Ethical MEL weighs the benefit of data against the rights and wellbeing of participants at every stage, from collection to disposal.

sections.title: Learning, Adaptive Management & Use of Evidence

questions.q: Utilization-focused evaluation (UFE), as developed by Michael Quinn Patton, is primarily organized around which guiding question?
options: How many indicators can be tracked at once?
How will the findings be used, and by whom?
How rigorous is the counterfactual design?
How much does the evaluation cost per beneficiary?
questions.explanation: UFE judges an evaluation's value by how its intended primary users actually use the findings, so use drives every design decision.

questions.q: In utilization-focused evaluation, the 'primary intended users' are best defined as:
options: All stakeholders who might read the report
The general public accessing an open data portal
Specific, identifiable people who will use the findings for decisions
questions.explanation: UFE requires naming real, specific people with the authority and interest to act on findings rather than an abstract audience.

questions.q: The acronym 'CLA' in adaptive programming stands for:
questions.explanation: USAID's CLA framework stands for Collaborating, Learning and Adapting, an approach to intentional, systematic programme improvement.

questions.q: A 'pause and reflect' session in adaptive management is best described as:
options: A mandatory audit of financial expenditure
A quarterly board meeting for governance decisions
A deliberate, structured moment for a team to make sense of data and adjust
A break in work with no documentation requirement
questions.explanation: Pause-and-reflect creates intentional space for teams to interpret evidence and decide on course corrections rather than rushing forward.

questions.q: An after-action review (AAR) traditionally centres on four questions. Which is NOT one of them?
options: Who should be held financially liable?
What can we learn and do differently next time?
questions.explanation: The AAR is a blameless learning tool comparing intent with reality to extract lessons, not to assign liability.

questions.q: A key principle that makes an after-action review effective is that it should be:
options: Held years after the activity concludes
Blame-free and focused on learning, not attribution of fault
questions.explanation: AARs work because participants speak candidly in a psychologically safe, blame-free space focused on improvement.

questions.q: A 'feedback loop' in a MEL system refers to:
options: A mechanism where information generated is fed back to inform decisions and action
The circular flow of funds between partners
A software bug that repeats data entry
questions.explanation: A feedback loop channels monitoring information back into decision-making so that learning changes subsequent action.

questions.q: Developmental evaluation (DE) is most appropriate for which situation?
options: A one-off compliance audit for a closed grant
Verifying pre-set targets in a routine service delivery contract
A stable, well-understood programme being scaled with a fixed model
Innovation in complex, dynamic conditions where the intervention is still evolving
questions.explanation: DE supports real-time adaptation of innovations under complexity and uncertainty, where the model is not yet fixed.

questions.q: A 'learning agenda' (or learning plan) is best understood as:
options: A list of mandatory donor compliance forms
The daily schedule of a training workshop
A set of prioritized questions an organization wants to answer to improve
A catalogue of every indicator in the logframe
questions.explanation: A learning agenda organizes a program's key knowledge gaps into prioritized questions that guide evidence generation and use.

questions.q: Real-time monitoring is distinguished from conventional monitoring primarily by:
options: Its avoidance of any digital tools
Its exclusive focus on end-line impact
The speed at which data are collected and made available for action
Its use of paper-based registers only
questions.explanation: Real-time monitoring shortens the lag between data collection and use so managers can act while it still matters.

questions.q: 'Closing the loop' with communities in feedback mechanisms specifically means:
options: Reporting back to communities what was heard and what action was taken
Ending community engagement once data are collected
Locking the complaints box at project end
Restricting feedback to written channels only
questions.explanation: Closing the loop means informing communities how their feedback was used, which builds trust and accountability.

questions.q: Knowledge management (KM) in a development organization primarily aims to:
options: Capture, share and apply knowledge so it improves practice
Archive documents so they are never accessed again
Replace all staff with automated systems
questions.explanation: KM systematizes how knowledge is captured, shared and reused so lessons inform future work rather than being lost.

questions.q: The distinction between 'tacit' and 'explicit' knowledge in KM is that tacit knowledge is:
options: Always more accurate than explicit knowledge
Written in manuals and easily codified
Experiential, personal and hard to articulate or document
questions.explanation: Tacit knowledge lives in people's experience and intuition and is difficult to codify, unlike documented explicit knowledge.

questions.q: 'Evidence uptake' refers to:
options: The extent to which research or evidence is absorbed and acted upon by decision-makers
The cost of commissioning an evaluation
The number of citations a study receives in journals
The volume of reports an organization produces
questions.explanation: Evidence uptake measures whether evidence actually reaches and influences the people making decisions.

questions.q: A common barrier to evidence use in the development sector is:
options: Evaluations being too short to read
Findings arriving after the decision window has closed
Too little data ever being collected
questions.explanation: Timeliness is critical; evidence that arrives after key decisions are made cannot influence them, undermining uptake.

questions.q: Adaptive management differs from traditional project management mainly in that it:
options: Focuses only on financial disbursement rates
Treats plans as hypotheses to be tested and revised as learning emerges
Eliminates the need for any monitoring
Fixes the implementation plan at design and never revises it
questions.explanation: Adaptive management uses ongoing evidence to test assumptions and adjust the intervention rather than rigidly following the original plan.

questions.q: In Patton's UFE, the 'personal factor' refers to:
options: The presence of an engaged, caring individual who takes ownership of using findings
The number of staff on the evaluation team
The evaluator's personal opinions overriding data
questions.explanation: The personal factor is Patton's finding that use rises sharply when a specific person cares about and champions the evaluation's use.

questions.q: Which of the following best exemplifies 'process use' of an evaluation?
options: Filing the report for audit purposes
Team members changing how they think and work because of engaging in the evaluation process itself
Publishing findings in an academic journal
questions.explanation: Process use is the learning and behaviour change that arises from participating in the evaluation, independent of the findings.

questions.q: A 'strategy testing' or 'strategy review' approach to adaptive management typically involves:
options: Locking the theory of change permanently at inception
Replacing staff who question the strategy
Periodically revisiting the theory of change and its assumptions against emerging evidence
questions.explanation: Strategy testing periodically checks whether the theory of change still holds against evidence and revises it if not.

questions.q: The 'Collaborating' dimension of CLA emphasizes:
options: Intentional internal and external coordination to share knowledge and reduce duplication
Working in isolation to protect intellectual property
Centralizing all decisions with the donor
Competing with peer organizations for funding
questions.explanation: Collaborating focuses on deliberate coordination and knowledge-sharing across teams and partners to strengthen results.

questions.q: In a learning agenda, prioritizing questions is important because:
options: Every possible question can and should be answered at once
Resources are limited, so effort should target the questions most useful for decisions
Prioritization removes the need for methods
questions.explanation: Prioritization ensures scarce evaluation resources address the knowledge gaps most consequential for programmatic decisions.

questions.q: A 'community scorecard' is a feedback tool that primarily:
options: Ranks staff performance for HR bonuses
Enables service users to assess services and dialogue with providers for improvement
questions.explanation: Community scorecards generate user assessments of services and structured interface with providers to drive local accountability and change.

questions.q: 'Sensemaking' in the context of MEL data refers to:
options: The collective interpretation of data to understand what it means for action
questions.explanation: Sensemaking is the collaborative process of interpreting evidence so a team can draw meaning and decide how to respond.

questions.q: One reason developmental evaluation resists producing a fixed 'final report' model is that:
options: The innovation keeps evolving, so evaluation provides ongoing feedback rather than a summative verdict
Reports are legally prohibited in DE
questions.explanation: DE embeds the evaluator in an evolving initiative to feed timely insights back, rather than delivering a one-time summative judgement.

questions.q: A 'most significant change' (MSC) technique contributes to learning by:
options: Collecting and collectively selecting significant change stories to surface what stakeholders value
questions.explanation: MSC gathers stories of significant change and uses structured selection to reveal what different stakeholders consider important.

questions.q: In adaptive management, treating programme assumptions as testable is important because:
options: It replaces the need for a theory of change
It guarantees the plan will not change
Assumptions may prove false, and testing them reveals when a course correction is needed
questions.explanation: Explicitly testing assumptions surfaces when the logic underpinning the intervention breaks down, prompting timely adaptation.

questions.q: 'Double-loop learning' (Argyris & Schon) differs from single-loop learning in that it:
options: Only corrects errors within existing assumptions
Doubles the number of indicators tracked
Questions and revises the underlying assumptions and goals, not just the actions
questions.explanation: Double-loop learning examines and adjusts the governing assumptions and objectives themselves, going beyond fixing surface actions.

questions.q: Which practice best demonstrates that an organization has an effective feedback loop from monitoring to management?
options: Monthly monitoring findings are reviewed and lead to documented decisions and adjustments
Monthly data are collected but stored unopened
Findings are sent solely to the donor
Data are shared only at project closure
questions.explanation: A functioning feedback loop is evidenced when monitoring data are regularly reviewed and demonstrably shape management decisions.

questions.q: The primary risk of NOT closing the loop with communities who give feedback is:
options: Erosion of trust and reduced willingness to provide future feedback
questions.explanation: When communities never hear how their input was used, they lose trust and disengage, undermining the feedback mechanism itself.

questions.q: A 'learning question' is well-formulated when it is:
options: Purely rhetorical with no intended use
Focused only on satisfying donor templates
Vague enough to allow any answer
Specific, answerable with available methods, and linked to a decision or action
questions.explanation: Good learning questions are precise, answerable, and tied to real decisions so the answers can be acted upon.

questions.q: In UFE, the evaluator's role is best characterized as:
options: An active facilitator who works with intended users to ensure findings are used
A detached, neutral outsider avoiding all stakeholder contact
A compliance inspector enforcing donor rules
questions.explanation: UFE evaluators actively facilitate engagement with intended users throughout to maximize the likelihood of use.

questions.q: 'Adaptive management' is sometimes contrasted with 'accountability' pressures because:
options: Rigid pre-set targets can discourage changing course even when evidence warrants it
Adaptation is always cheaper than accountability
Accountability requires no data at all
questions.explanation: Fixed targets and rigid results frameworks can create tension with adaptation, penalizing teams that change plans based on learning.

questions.q: A 'knowledge broker' in the evidence-to-use pathway primarily:
options: Only stores documents in an archive
Sells research findings to the highest bidder
Connects evidence producers with decision-makers and translates findings into usable form
Blocks access to evidence for competitive advantage
questions.explanation: Knowledge brokers bridge the gap between research and practice, translating and connecting evidence to those who can use it.

questions.q: Which of the following is a hallmark of a strong organizational learning culture?
options: Sharing only success stories externally and internally
Psychological safety that allows honest discussion of what is not working
questions.explanation: Psychological safety lets teams surface failures and problems honestly, which is essential for genuine organizational learning.

questions.q: 'Real-time monitoring' during a humanitarian response is especially valuable because:
options: It focuses only on post-crisis academic study
It reduces the need to consult affected people
It allows rapid course correction while needs are changing quickly
It eliminates the need for any baseline
questions.explanation: In fast-moving crises, real-time data enable responders to adjust delivery while conditions and needs shift.

questions.q: A 'pause and reflect' meeting produces the most value when it:
options: Reviews data but reaches no decisions
Results in concrete, documented adaptations and clear ownership
questions.explanation: Reflection translates into value only when it yields specific decisions and assigned responsibility for follow-through.

questions.q: In the context of evidence use, 'conceptual use' of an evaluation means:
options: Findings are used only for public relations
Findings directly change a specific programme decision
Findings shift how people understand an issue over time, even without immediate action
questions.explanation: Conceptual use is the gradual influence of evidence on understanding and framing, distinct from direct instrumental use.

questions.q: 'Instrumental use' of an evaluation is best illustrated by:
options: A team using findings to make a specific, concrete decision or change
An academic referencing the study in a lecture
A manager citing findings to justify continuing existing practice unchanged
questions.explanation: Instrumental use occurs when evidence directly informs a specific decision or action.

questions.q: A well-designed community feedback mechanism should be:
options: Available only via a single online portal
Anonymous only to staff, not to community members
Accessible, safe, and offer multiple channels appropriate to the context
questions.explanation: Effective feedback mechanisms are accessible, safe, and offer varied channels so all groups, including the marginalized, can participate.

questions.q: In adaptive programming, a 'learning-by-doing' or iterative approach is often summarized as:
options: Wait for the final evaluation before changing anything
Test, learn, adapt in short cycles
questions.explanation: Iterative adaptation proceeds through short cycles of testing, learning and adjusting rather than a single upfront master plan.

questions.q: Which South Asian context factor commonly strengthens the case for adaptive management?
options: High contextual complexity and volatility across states and districts
Perfectly predictable political and monsoon conditions
questions.explanation: The region's high heterogeneity and volatility across sub-national contexts make rigid blueprints risky and favour adaptation.

questions.q: A key difference between developmental evaluation and formative evaluation is that DE:
options: Improves a fixed, defined model before rollout
Only occurs after a programme ends
Never involves the evaluator with the team
Supports the ongoing creation and evolution of an innovation under complexity
questions.explanation: Formative evaluation refines a defined model, whereas DE accompanies the emergence and continuous evolution of an innovation.

questions.q: When an organization builds a 'learning agenda' with a donor, a major benefit is:
options: It locks the programme into never adapting
Shared prioritized questions align evidence generation with decisions both parties care about
It guarantees funding regardless of results
It replaces the need for any monitoring plan
questions.explanation: A co-created learning agenda aligns evidence efforts to the questions that matter for both implementer and funder decisions.

questions.q: The phrase 'analysis paralysis' in adaptive management warns against:
options: Acting too quickly without any data
Collecting and debating data endlessly without ever making decisions
questions.explanation: Analysis paralysis is the failure to decide because a team keeps analyzing indefinitely, defeating the purpose of timely adaptation.

questions.q: A practical way to institutionalize reflection is to:
options: Wait for the final evaluation to reflect
Delegate all reflection to external consultants
Schedule recurring pause-and-reflect sessions with a clear agenda and follow-up
Rely on ad hoc conversations only when a crisis hits
questions.explanation: Embedding regular, structured reflection sessions with follow-up makes learning a routine practice rather than an accident.

questions.q: In evidence uptake, 'demand-side' factors refer to:
options: The capacity, incentives and openness of decision-makers to seek and use evidence
The quality and timeliness of the research produced
questions.explanation: Demand-side factors concern users' willingness, incentives and ability to seek out and apply evidence in decisions.

questions.q: A monitoring dashboard best supports adaptive management when it:
options: Highlights a few decision-relevant indicators with clear thresholds for action
Is updated once at project end
Displays hundreds of indicators with no interpretation
Is accessible only to the finance team
questions.explanation: Dashboards drive adaptation when they focus attention on a manageable set of decision-relevant signals with actionable thresholds.

questions.q: 'Positive deviance' as a learning approach identifies:
options: Outliers to be excluded from analysis
Staff who deviate from financial rules
Individuals or units achieving better outcomes than peers under the same constraints, to learn from them
questions.explanation: Positive deviance studies those who succeed despite similar conditions to surface replicable local solutions.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the relationship between monitoring and learning?
options: Learning replaces the need for monitoring
Monitoring generates data, but learning requires deliberate reflection and sensemaking
Monitoring data automatically produce learning without interpretation
Learning only happens in formal evaluations
questions.explanation: Data alone do not create learning; teams must deliberately interpret and reflect on monitoring information to learn.

questions.q: A common pitfall when scaling an innovation validated by developmental evaluation is:
options: Continuing to gather feedback in new sites
Assuming the emergent model will work identically in every new context without further adaptation
questions.explanation: Because DE-supported innovations are context-sensitive, assuming faithful replication without local adaptation risks failure at scale.

questions.q: In Edward Tufte's terminology, the 'data-ink ratio' refers to the proportion of a graphic's ink devoted to what?
questions.explanation: The data-ink ratio is the share of ink used to present the actual, non-redundant data, which Tufte argues should be maximized.

questions.q: A donor report shows a bar chart whose y-axis starts at 60 rather than 0, exaggerating the difference between two bars. This is an example of what?
options: A truncated axis that inflates the visual lie factor
Correct use of a logarithmic scale
questions.explanation: Truncating the baseline of a bar chart visually exaggerates differences, increasing what Tufte calls the 'lie factor'.

questions.q: Which chart type is most appropriate for showing how a single total is divided among a small number of mutually exclusive categories at one point in time?
options: A pie or stacked bar chart
